stories.headline: House Dem leader's attack on voter ID comes back to haunt him after election fraud bust in his home state
stories.note: An election fraud bust in his own state undercuts the Democratic leader's attack on voter ID.
body: Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, the chairman of the House Democratic Caucus and the party's No. 3 leader in the House, is taking heat for opposing a voter ID measure on California's November ballot.

Proposition 39 would require voters to show a government-issued photo ID at the polls. At a press event earlier this month with Democratic governor candidate Xavier Becerra, Aguilar called it a Republican "voter suppression effort" and warned that small mistakes or name changes could cost people their votes.
Weeks later, the Justice Department announced charges against several lawful permanent residents in California accused of registering to vote even though they aren't citizens.

California Republicans Ken Calvert, Vince Fong and Young Kim pounced, pointing out that Americans already show ID to board a plane, rent a car or pick up a prescription. Fong said the DOJ bust "is exactly why these safeguards matter."
Newsom's office pushed back on the DOJ case, citing reports that more of those charged were registered Republicans than Democrats and noting that courts have rejected claims of widespread fraud.

Why it matters: Voter ID is popular nationally and already law in 36 states, so a fraud case landing in California right before the vote gives Republicans a timely argument against a top Democratic leader.

stories.headline: Newsom spars with Trump-appointed prosecutor over 20,000 suspected noncitizens on voter rolls
stories.note: Newsom is on defense over roughly 20,000 suspected noncitizens on California's voter rolls.
body: Gov. Gavin Newsom's office and Bill Essayli, the Trump-appointed first assistant U.S. attorney in California's Central District, traded shots online this week over whether the state does enough to keep noncitizens from voting.

The fight centers on a Justice Department lawsuit asking California to verify the citizenship of more than 20,000 registered voters that federal immigration data flagged as likely noncitizens. Those voters were mailed ballots starting Oct. 1.

In a court filing, a Los Angeles County election official said the registrar's office isn't set up to verify citizenship beyond a voter's own sworn statement. Essayli called that a "massive concession," writing that "American citizens' votes are being diluted."

Newsom's office answered that California follows federal law requiring registrants to swear under penalty of perjury that they are citizens, and mocked Essayli's title. The county also argued the DOJ list is unreliable, saying many sampled records were canceled or inactive.

Essayli said those numbers mean little since the county admits it can't verify citizenship. The DOJ has already charged 28 lawful permanent residents from the list with fraudulently registering, and officials say most of them voted.
Why it matters: With ballots already being counted, the case puts Newsom and California Democrats on defense over election integrity heading into the midterms.

stories.headline: El-Sayed's past Muslim Brotherhood comments raise red flags as he eyes powerful role
stories.note: Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's past comments become a liability in a key Senate race.
body: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed is facing new scrutiny over a 2011 op-ed in which he urged the Obama administration to back Egyptian protesters tied to the Muslim Brotherhood.

The issue resurfaced after Jordan Domingue, his security chief during his 2018 run for governor, said El-Sayed badly wants a seat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee despite having no foreign policy experience.

Two Republicans on that committee pushed back hard. Sen. Mike Lee said a candidate who cheered the Brotherhood's rise in Egypt "should not come anywhere near the U.S. Senate." Sen. Dave McCormick said someone with El-Sayed's "radical views has no business on it."

El-Sayed recently said at a town hall that he disavows the Muslim Brotherhood, but his campaign didn't respond to Fox News Digital's questions about the op-ed. He has also tried to distance himself from the party's socialist wing despite appearing with streamer Hasan Piker.
Why it matters: El-Sayed is running on affordability, and Republicans are working to make his past foreign policy views the story in a Michigan race that could decide control of the Senate.

stories.headline: 'Fire every commissioner': Minnesota GOP nominee vows sweeping purge over fraud
stories.note: The GOP nominee keeps Walz-era fraud front and center in Minnesota's governor race.
body: Minnesota's fraud scandals took center stage again in the governor's race as Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth and Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar met for their second debate of the week.
Demuth promised to fire every state commissioner on her first day and replace them with experts who will bring accountability. "We have to change the culture of fraud," she said.

Klobuchar called the plan "absurd" and said she helped get the U.S. attorney more prosecutors once the fraud came to light. She also took a swipe at outgoing Gov. Tim Walz, saying he "should have caught the fraud earlier."

Demuth countered that Klobuchar hasn't named any specific policies where she'd break from Walz, whom Klobuchar has called an "incredible governor." Klobuchar, for her part, accused Demuth of being a rubber stamp for President Trump.
The two also sparred over spending, regulation and public safety. Either way the state will elect its first female governor, and a Demuth win would also make her Minnesota's first Black governor.
Why it matters: Fraud under a Democratic administration is the defining issue of the race, forcing Klobuchar to criticize her own party's governor while Demuth runs as the reformer.

stories.headline: France in flames is preview of what 'DSA' Democrats want for US, senator warns
stories.note: A GOP senator ties France's riots to the Democratic Socialists' agenda.
body: Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., says the riots, fires and looting sweeping France are a warning about where Democrats want to take America. "That's exactly what they want here, the DSA Democrats," he told Fox News Digital.
The unrest in France began as protests over living costs and strained public services before turning violent, leading to curfews in parts of Paris and other cities.

Schmitt warned that a Democratic House could threaten ICE funding and stall Republican work on immigration, permitting and regulations. He contrasted that with results in Missouri he credits to working with the Trump administration.

He pointed to Boeing landing the Air Force's F-47 and Navy's F/A-XX fighter programs, which he said would bring 7,000 direct jobs, and to Operation Show Me Justice, an ATF-led surge that the Justice Department says produced 435 arrests and 166 firearms seized in St. Louis.
Schmitt cast the midterms as "common sense versus crazy" but said Republicans can't take any vote for granted, predicting the GOP will hold the Senate while the House is up for grabs.
Why it matters: Republicans are pairing a law-and-order warning with concrete jobs and crime wins as they make their closing case to voters.
